claims.text: V-Cr-Ti-based refractory alloys exhibit low activation under fusion-relevant neutron irradiation.
V-Cr-Ti-based refractory alloys retain stable high-temperature mechanical properties under fusion-relevant neutron irradiation.
V-Cr-Ti-based alloys are suitable structural materials for fusion-reactor plasma-facing components.
The proposed initial material is a homogenized, solutionized V-Cr-Ti-based alloy.
Temperatures of approximately 600–900 °C under high vacuum are typical of fusion-reactor plasma-facing environments.
Stable solid-solution phases form in the irradiated alloy.
Stable solid-solution phases inhibit radiation-induced defects.
Stable solid-solution phases reduce grain-boundary embrittlement.
The constituent elements of V-Cr-Ti-based alloys produce short-lived radioactive isotopes.
V-Cr-Ti-based alloys remain stable under high neutron flux.
Short-lived activation products limit long-term radiological hazards.
Stability under high neutron flux enables the alloy to maintain mechanical integrity at elevated temperatures.
Irradiated V-Cr-Ti-based alloys will have significantly lower residual radioactivity than irradiated pure tungsten.
Irradiated V-Cr-Ti-based alloys will retain superior mechanical stability compared with pure tungsten.
Standard tungsten-based plasma-facing components exhibit higher induced radioactivity than V-Cr-Ti-based alloys.
Standard tungsten-based plasma-facing components exhibit reduced ductility at elevated temperatures.
The stability of V-Cr-Ti-based alloys above 1200 °C or under extremely high neutron flux has not been confirmed.
Empirical data on the long-duration mechanical and activation behavior of V-Cr-Ti-based alloys in fusion environments are limited.
